strengths: Clear motivation: extending reasoning-based medical image segmentation from isolated single-round queries to multi-round dialogues with cross-turn entity dependencies is practical and valuable for interactive clinical workflows.

Comprehensive benchmark: the authors construct MR-MedSeg comprising 177K multi-turn conversations across 168 categories and 9 imaging modalities, addressing a genuine data void in interactive medical vision-language modeling.

Well-structured framework: the proposed MediRound effectively incorporates historical dialogue context, cropped entity regions, and bounding box tokens to enable chained multi-turn reasoning, supported by solid experimental gains across multiple metrics.
weaknesses: Critical technical omissions for JCM: The Judgment & Correction Mechanism (JCM) is introduced as one of the core technical novelties to mitigate error propagation, yet the main manuscript completely omits the training objectives, target definitions, and loss functions for both MLPJ and MLPC, simply deferring to an absent appendix. As a core contribution, its mathematical formulation and supervision signal should be explicitly detailed.

Unclear baseline training details: It is ambiguous whether baselines such as SegLLM-7B/13B were fully fine-tuned on MR-MedSeg using identical training setups or evaluated zero-shot/off-the-shelf. If SegLLM was not re-trained on this domain-specific dataset, the claim of superiority over prior multi-round frameworks is compromised.

Factual and citation inconsistencies: The paper repeatedly references 'GPT-5' throughout Section 3 and Figure 3 for data generation and refinement, citing reference [1] ('GPT-4 technical report'). Citing non-existent or unreleased models reflects careless drafting and raises questions regarding the exact generation setup and reproducibility.

Synthetic conversation bias: The dataset construction relies heavily on template filling and LLM expansions around predefined anatomical/spatial relationships from SA-Med2D-20M. There is limited validation of whether these synthetic dialogue chains accurately mimic actual multi-round clinical workflows or physician question habits in real-world diagnostic settings.

strengths: Meaningful and practical task formulation: MEMR-Seg extends medical reasoning segmentation into a multi-turn, interactive paradigm where subsequent queries depend on previously segmented anatomical entities, closely aligning with real clinical workflows.

Substantial benchmark construction: The MR-MedSeg dataset contributes over 177K multi-round dialogues spanning 168 medical categories and 9 modalities, structured across five well-categorized clinical relationship archetypes (e.g., organ-lesion, anatomical stratification, functional attribute relationships).

Effective error-mitigation strategy: Addressing the critical vulnerability of cascading errors in sequential segmentation, the Judgment & Correction Mechanism (JCM) provides an efficient, plug-and-play module to assess and refine [SEG] token embeddings at inference time.

Thorough experimental validation: The authors compare against a diverse range of baselines—including human-assisted tools, two-stage MLLM + specialist segmentation pipelines, and general multi-round models (SegLLM)—demonstrating consistent performance gains across both overall metrics and per-round trajectories.
weaknesses: Factual/editorial inconsistencies regarding generation tools: The text repeatedly references 'GPT-5' for dataset generation and refinement (Sec. 1, Sec. 3, Sec. 4) while citing the GPT-4 technical report [1]. This is either an editorial error or an inaccurate naming convention that should be corrected.

Lack of essential training details for JCM in the main text: While Algorithm 1 clearly outlines inference, the training objective and supervision signal for the Quality Judgment Module ($MLP_J$) and Correction Module ($MLP_C$) are insufficiently detailed in the main body (e.g., defining how ground-truth quality labels $q$ are formulated from IoU/Dice and what loss function optimizes $MLP_C$).

Missing comparisons to exposure bias mitigation baselines: The discrepancy between teacher forcing during training and free-running inference is well-known in multi-turn modeling. The paper introduces JCM at inference time, but does not compare against standard training-time mitigation strategies, such as scheduled sampling or training with jittered/noisy reference masks.

Potential synthetic template bias: Because dialogues are generated via semi-automated templates and LLM expansion, there is a risk of stylistic rigidity. Evaluation on an independently collected, unprompted clinician dialogue set would further validate clinical real-world generalizability.

strengths: Addresses an important and practical problem in interactive medical imaging by formalizing the Multi-Round Entity-Level Medical Reasoning Segmentation (MEMR-Seg) task.
Constructs MR-MedSeg, a comprehensive dataset covering 177K multi-round dialogues, 118K images, 168 categories, and 9 imaging modalities across five well-categorized clinical relationship scenarios.
Provides extensive experimental comparisons against both single-stage multi-round models (SegLLM) and two-stage LLM/MLLM + medical segmenter pipelines across multiple turns.
The paper is generally well-structured with informative diagrams (e.g., Figures 1, 2, and 4) clearly illustrating the task setup and data taxonomy.
weaknesses: Crucial technical details regarding the Judgment & Correction Mechanism (JCM) are omitted from the main text. While JCM is highlighted as a primary technical contribution to combat error propagation, there is no mathematical formulation of the training loss, target labels for MLPJ (e.g., how feature quality is quantified), or supervision signal for the correction module MLPC, making the method difficult to evaluate for technical soundness and reproducibility.

The baseline labeled 'Human-Thinking' in Tables 1 and 2 is insufficiently explained. It is unclear how human experts were deployed across the 1,270+ multi-round test conversations, what instructions they followed, or how experimental consistency was maintained.

The core baseline architecture of MediRound closely follows SegLLM (Wang et al., 2024), adapting it by swapping general components for domain-specific backbones (LLaVA-Med and MedSAM); hence, the architectural novelty is somewhat incremental.
The manuscript repeatedly mentions using 'GPT-5' (citing Achiam et al. [1], which is the GPT-4 Technical Report), which appears to be a careless factual error/hallucination in the text.

The ablation studies are somewhat limited: while backbones and the threshold parameter beta are analyzed, there is no component-wise ablation dissecting the contributions of the cropped image feature, bounding box projection, and full dialogue history.

strengths: Clear clinical motivation: The paper targets multi-round entity-level reasoning segmentation (MEMR-Seg), a practical yet under-explored setting where users iteratively query organs, sub-structures, and lesions with reference to prior segmentation outputs.

Comprehensive benchmark construction: The authors build MR-MedSeg with 177K dialogues spanning 5 distinct interaction paradigms (anatomical stratification, organ-lesion association, spatial, inferential, and attribute relationships) across 9 imaging modalities and 168 entity classes.

Effective error-mitigation design: The proposed Judgment & Correction Mechanism (JCM) provides a lightweight, post-hoc method to detect and correct degraded [SEG] representations during sequential multi-round rollouts, effectively addressing error propagation.

Strong empirical results: MediRound outperforms both multi-stage baselines (e.g., MLLMs combined with medical segmenters) and adapted natural-image methods (SegLLM) by noticeable margins across all conversation turns, supported by informative per-round analyses and ablation studies.
weaknesses: Template dependency and conversational realism: The multi-round dialogues are synthesized using 50–80 templates per relationship generated via LLMs. The paper lacks evaluation on spontaneous, free-form clinical dialogue or clinician-in-the-loop user studies, leaving open questions regarding out-of-distribution language robustness.

Internal evaluation scope: The evaluation is conducted on splits derived from the same source distribution (SA-Med2D-20M). Cross-dataset validation on unseen external clinical datasets would strengthen the claims of generalizability.

Correction module design constraints: The correction module MLPc operates strictly as a feed-forward mapping on the latent embedding hc without re-attending to visual features or grounding queries, which may limit the ceiling of feature restoration for severely degraded predictions.

Terminology inconsistency: The text repeatedly refers to 'GPT-5' for data generation (e.g., in Section 3 and Figure 3), while citation [1] references the GPT-4 technical report; this should be corrected or clarified.

strengths: Formulates a practical and timely task, MEMR-Seg (Multi-Round Entity-Level Medical Reasoning Segmentation), addressing iterative cross-turn reasoning in medical segmentation scenarios.

Introduces MR-MedSeg, a substantial benchmark containing 177K multi-round conversations covering 5 distinct clinical relationship types (organ-lesion, anatomical hierarchy, attribute, spatial, and inferential) across multiple modalities.
Proposes a sensible and effective post-hoc Judgment & Correction Mechanism (JCM) that specifically tackles error accumulation across dialogue turns without requiring full end-to-end retraining.

Conducts thorough empirical evaluations comparing MediRound against specialist models with human-in-the-loop guidance, multi-stage MLLM + segmentor baselines, and general multi-round models (SegLLM), demonstrating clear improvements.
weaknesses: The core model design heavily mirrors existing general-domain multi-round reasoning segmentation frameworks like SegLLM (concatenating cropped reference visual features, bbox embeddings, and conversational text into an MLLM), with the primary novelty lying in the medical domain adaptation and the lightweight JCM module.

The dialogue generation pipeline relies on template integration and LLM expansion; while filtered by experts, the linguistic diversity may remain somewhat constrained to specific prompt structures compared to free-form clinical interactions.

The JCM operates strictly in feature space (transforming the [SEG] token hidden representation via MLPs) rather than re-attending to visual/spatial evidence, which inherently limits its ability to correct severe localization failures or completely missed targets.

The framework is currently restricted to 2D slices and single-object predictions per turn, which partially limits its clinical utility for 3D volumetric scans (e.g., volumetric CT/MRI) common in clinical workflows.

strengths: Significance of the task formulation: Extending reasoning-based segmentation to multi-round medical conversations (MEMR-Seg) addresses a practical clinical challenge where subsequent diagnostic and segmentation targets depend hierarchically, spatially, or etiologically on previously identified entities.

Substantial dataset contribution: MR-MedSeg provides 177K multi-turn conversations covering 168 medical categories across 9 imaging modalities, categorized into five clear clinical interaction patterns (e.g., organ-lesion, anatomical hierarchy, spatial relations).

Effective mechanism for error accumulation: The Judgment & Correction Mechanism (JCM) provides an interesting and computationally lightweight post-training strategy to estimate feature quality and refine the [SEG] token representation during inference, mitigating compounding errors across conversation turns.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: The paper conducts extensive comparisons against both human-assisted single-round segmentation tools, cascaded MLLM + specialist segmentation models, and multi-round models (SegLLM), demonstrating clear improvements across metrics (Dice, gIoU, cIoU) across up to 8 conversation rounds.
weaknesses: Incremental architectural novelty: The overall framework closely follows SegLLM and LISA-style paradigms, where bounding boxes and cropped patches of previously segmented targets are fed alongside text instructions to an MLLM (LLaVA-Med) and decoded via a promptable segmenter (MedSAM).

Data generation realism and questionable references: The dataset construction relies heavily on predefined templates (50–80 per relation) and synthetic generation using an unreleased or mislabeled model referred to as 'GPT-5' throughout the manuscript. This raises questions regarding both terminology accuracy and whether the generated dialogues exhibit sufficient diversity and natural variability compared to real clinical dialogues.

Fairness of baseline comparisons: In Table 1, standard MLLM baselines (e.g., GPT-4o, Gemini-2.5, Qwen3-VL combined with MediSee or IMIS-Net) are evaluated in a decoupled, prompt-based pipeline without task-specific fine-tuning. It remains ambiguous whether competing multi-round models such as SegLLM were fine-tuned on the 174K training set of MR-MedSeg or tested out-of-the-box.

Technical soundness and potential collapse in JCM: The Correction Module (MLPC) is an MLP trained on top of frozen features to output a representation that minimizes segmentation mask loss against the ground truth. The paper provides limited insight into whether MLPC generalizes well across unseen out-of-distribution errors or tends to overfit, given that an isolated MLP does not cross-attend back to image features or text contexts.
